title: A Tale of Two Bens: What Happens When We Decide a Child's Future at 14?
author: Joel Kenyon
summary: Teacher and writer Joel Kenyon uses the real story of a former student, given the pseudonym Ben, to argue against proposals that would let 14-year-olds opt out of GCSEs into vocational tracks. In the true account, Ben overcame a chaotic home life and low predicted grades to leave school with five good GCSEs, eventually becoming the first in his family to attend university. Kenyon then rewrites the same student's story under a hypothetical system where Ben, flagged early as at-risk, is steered at 14 into a bricklaying course instead of completing his GCSEs — a decision that later locks him out of jobs, further study, and the university path he took in reality. The piece is less a policy paper than a narrative thought experiment showing how early tracking compounds disadvantage for exactly the students it claims to help. Kenyon's central argument is that the current system, whatever its flaws, preserves full optionality at 16, while proposals to choose vocational pathways at 13 or 14 remove that optionality before students are equipped to exercise it wisely. He frames this as a matter of doors staying open versus doors closing years before a young person can foresee the consequences.
points: Uses a real former student's dual-outcome story — one true, one hypothetical — to make an abstract policy debate about 14-year-old tracking concrete and human.
Argues that being flagged early as at-risk (NEET) too often converts into reduced expectations and narrowed pathways rather than genuine additional support.
Shows how a 14-year-old's vocational choice, made without real understanding of its consequences, becomes a labor-market barrier at 16 when GCSE-holding peers are given hiring priority.
Contrasts the current 16-plus system, which preserves full choice among A-Levels, apprenticeships, or work, with early-tracking proposals that close those doors years earlier.
Frames locking a whole cohort of students into narrow pathways based on early disadvantage as a policy that entrenches rather than solves the problem it targets.
quotes: His dad was injured at work and had been out of work since Ben was 10 years old. To pay for food, school uniforms and the roof over his head, his mum was forced to work two jobs.
Ben, by his sheer will and determination, left Year 11 with 5 GCSEs grade C and above. He even got a B in Maths. He was one of only 35% of pupils at our school to do so.
On paper, this was supposed to offer him more support, but in reality, it served very little to offer him any help.
He applied to work at O'Riley's but they required a grade 4 in Maths and English, he didn't even have a grade 1.
Moving this choice to the point before they get their GCSEs, never mind the fact they are only 13 or 14 when they do choose, is putting up walls that today, do not exist.

Making it so pupils could actually leave school with a good set of GCSEs based on a decision at 14, that will take years to rectify if they discover they made the wrong one, is setting a whole generation of young adults to be locked in, with very little ability to move.
